newsitem.title: USA: Fed sees muted inflation in growing economy.
newsitem.headline: Fed sees muted inflation in growing economy.

text.p: The economy kept growing moderately during November with little or no sign of wage and price pressures flaring up, the Federal Reserve said on Wednesday.

The Fed's latest Beige Book summary of national economic activity appeared to suggest that slow but steady expansion, rather than an acceleration, lies ahead, so there would be little need for interest-rate rises to dampen inflation risks.

"Moderate economic growth continues to be reported in nearly all Federal Reserve districts," said the summary prepared by the Philadelphia Fed for the Dec. 17 meeting of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee, which will plot interest-rate strategy.

The Fed report, based on interviews with businessmen in all 12 Fed districts conducted before Nov. 23, did not reveal strong concern that either wages or prices were rising so rapidly as to pose a threat to the 5-1/2-year-old economic expansion.

It said skilled workers were in short supply across the country yet there was no widespread pickup in wage demands. Similarly, retail prices remained stable despite more costly raw materials in some regions.

The Dec. 17 meeting of the policy-setting FOMC is the final one this year. Recent reports showing surprisingly strong construction spending and a manufacturing surge had caused some speculation that growth might be picking up after a slow third quarter.
Analysts said the key would be whether consumers, who fuel two-thirds of national economic activity, spend lavishly or frugally during the holiday shopping period from Thanksgiving through Christmas.

The Fed summary said retailers were "modestly optimistic" about holiday sales but did not anticipate a boom in business. It said price discounting was increasing in Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Celeveland as merchants kept inventories in line with sales.
Retailers in the Boston, New York and Phildelphia Fed regions were anticipating gains in holiday sales ranging from 2 percent to 6 percent over last year.
"In St. Louis, Kansas City, Dallas and San Francisco the season is expected to be strong," the regional Fed banks reported.
The previous Beige Book, issued on Oct. 30, similarly noted tight labour markets. But the latest Fed summary said strong hiring did not seem to be translating into big wage demands.

"Reports ... do not indicate a generalized acceleration in wage increases despite growing reports of labour shortages," the central bank summary said. Skilled trades workers and specialised technical employees were reported in particularly short supply.
The Fed summary said there has been "virtually no change" in retail prices in recent weeks, although there was some firming in raw materials costs and in prices for intermediate goods.
The regional Fed banks in Richmond, Va., as well as in Atlanta, Kansas City and Dallas, said their manufacturing and construction material costs were on the rise.

Manufacturing activity kept growing during October and November. Most said the pickup was modest, though the Boston Fed said manufacturers there were reporting gains of up to 15 percent in their orders and revenues.
